02  /  The short version

Five things to know before you build

01

An agent is a model running in a loop.

It picks its own next step, calls tools, reads the result, and repeats until the task is done or a stop condition fires.

02

Start simpler than you think.

Anthropic's advice is the simplest solution that works. Many apps need only one well-prompted call with retrieval.

03

Claude gives you four ways to run one.

Write the loop on the Messages API, embed the Agent SDK, use the Claude Code CLI, or host it on Managed Agents.

04

Tools decide quality.

Clear tool descriptions, small token-efficient outputs and real evals matter more than framework choice.

05

Plan for cost, drift and oversight.

Agents use about 4x the tokens of chat, multi-agent systems about 15x, and errors compound over long runs.

03  /  Definition

An agent is a model in a loop with tools

The working definition

An agent plans its own steps and calls tools, using what each tool returns as ground truth to decide what to do next. It runs until the task is complete, it needs a human, or a limit such as a maximum number of iterations is hit.

Workflow

The LLM and tools are orchestrated by predefined code paths. You decide the steps.

Agent

The LLM directs its own process and tool use. The model decides the steps.

In practice

Most agents are simply an LLM using tools based on environmental feedback, in a loop. The implementation is often straightforward. The hard part is designing the tools and the guardrails around them.

04  /  The spectrum

Climb one rung at a time

1

Single LLM call

One prompt, one answer. Tune with retrieval and in-context examples.

Control
You control everything
Cost and latency
Lowest
Example
Summarize, classify, extract
2

Augmented LLM

A call enhanced with retrieval, tools and memory. The model writes its own queries.

Control
You wire the tools
Cost and latency
Low
Example
Q&A over your docs
3

Workflow

Several calls on predefined paths: chain, route, parallelize, orchestrate, evaluate.

Control
Your code is in charge
Cost and latency
Medium
Example
Draft, check, then translate
4

Agent

The model chooses steps and tools in a loop, with environmental feedback each turn.

Control
The model is in charge
Cost and latency
Highest
Example
Fix a bug across many files
more predictablemore flexible
Anthropic's guidance Find the simplest solution possible and add complexity only when needed. Agentic systems trade latency and cost for better task performance, so ask whether that trade is worth it for your task.

05  /  Anatomy

Six parts make an agent

1

Model

Claude does the reasoning: reads context, chooses a tool, decides when it is finished.

2

Instructions

System prompt and task: role, constraints, definition of done, how to report.

3

Tools

Functions you define, built-ins like bash and file edit, server tools like web search, and MCP servers.

4

Context and memory

The window, plus compaction, notes written to files, and just-in-time retrieval.

5

Harness

The loop itself: tool execution, permissions, hooks, sandbox, stop conditions, logging.

6

Environment

Files, APIs, browsers, tests. Whatever returns ground truth after each action.

Photo: Ingo Dierking, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Rule of thumb Each part is a place to simplify. Anthropic's three principles: keep the design simple, show the agent's planning steps, and invest in the agent-computer interface, meaning tool docs and testing.

Managed Agents concepts

Four objects: an Agent (model, prompt, tools, MCP servers, skills), an Environment (where it runs), a Session (one running instance) and Events (messages in and out, streamed over SSE).

Same loop, different owner

The Agent SDK, Claude Code and Managed Agents share the idea of a built-in agent loop with context management such as prompt caching and compaction. What changes is who hosts and operates it.

Heads up

Managed Agents is in beta, so features and limits can change. Check the current docs before committing a design to it.

07  /  Capabilities

Tools, MCP and Skills extend what Claude can do

Tools

Tools differ by where the code runs.

Client tools

Your functions plus Anthropic-defined schemas like bash and text_editor. Claude returns stop_reason: "tool_use"; your code runs it and sends back a tool_result.

Server tools

web_search, web_fetch, code_execution, tool_search. Anthropic runs them and returns results in the same response.

MCP

The Model Context Protocol is an open standard, introduced by Anthropic in November 2024, for connecting AI assistants to the systems where data lives: repositories, business tools, development environments.

Write one client integration and reach a growing ecosystem of servers, instead of one custom connector per source.

Supported in the Agent SDK and in Managed Agents agent definitions.

Skills

Skills are folders of instructions, metadata and optional scripts or templates that Claude loads on demand, so guidance does not have to be repeated in every prompt.

Anthropic provides pre-built Skills for PowerPoint, Excel, Word and PDF work. You can write your own for your domain.

Skills load from .claude/ in Agent SDK projects.

# What Claude sends when it wants a tool
{"type": "tool_use", "id": "toolu_01...", "name": "get_weather", "input": {"location": "San Francisco, CA"}}
# What your code sends back
{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": "toolu_01...", "content": "15 degrees Celsius, partly cloudy"}

08  /  Use cases

Where agents already work: code and support

Use case 01

Coding agents

Edit across many files, run commands, read test output, and iterate until it passes.

  • Verifiable: automated tests say whether it worked
  • Tight feedback loop: test results drive the next attempt
  • Well-defined, structured problem space
  • Objective quality measure, so evals are practical
  • Anthropic reports agents solving real GitHub issues on SWE-bench Verified from the pull request description alone
  • Human review still matters for fit with the wider system
Try Claude Code in the terminal, or the Agent SDK for your own tooling
Use case 02

Customer support

Chat that can also act: look up an order, issue a refund, update a ticket.

  • Conversation and action in one flow
  • Tools can pull customer data, order history and knowledge articles
  • Success is clear: the issue is resolved
  • Hand off to a human at defined points
  • Some teams price per resolved conversation, which rewards effectiveness
  • Keep humans in the loop for refunds above a limit
Try Routing: easy questions to a small model, hard ones to a stronger one

09  /  Use cases

Research, documents, operations and integrations

Research agents

A lead agent plans, then spawns parallel subagents that each search, read and condense findings. Anthropic's Research feature works this way.

Best for breadth-first questions with many independent directions.

Built withSubagents, web search, memory, evals

Document and data work

Skills for PowerPoint, Excel, Word and PDF let an agent build, edit and analyze files, using code execution to do the work.

Best for repeatable report and spreadsheet workflows.

Built withSkills, code execution, file tools

Ops and back office

Managed Agents can read files, run commands, browse the web and run code in a sandbox, and can run on a cron schedule.

Best for recurring, long-running chores with a clear output.

Built withManaged Agents, sandboxes, schedules

Tool-rich assistants

Connect Slack, Drive, issue trackers or your own APIs over MCP, so the agent works where your data already is.

Best when the value is in the integrations.

Built withMCP servers, tool search, permissions

10  /  Fit test

Does the task actually need an agent?

✓

The path is not known in advance

You cannot list the steps up front. Number of files, searches or retries varies by task.

✓

It needs action, not just an answer

Value comes from doing: editing, querying, filing, sending, with tools.

✓

Success is checkable

Tests pass, the ticket is resolved, the numbers reconcile. Anything you can verify automatically.

✓

There is a feedback loop

Each action returns real signal the agent can use to correct itself.

✓

Cost and latency are acceptable

Plan for several model calls per task. Multi-agent runs multiply that.

✓

Humans can oversee it

There are checkpoints, approvals or review before consequential actions.

Decision path

Can one good call with retrieval do it?
Yes: stop here. No agent needed.
Are the steps fixed and known?
Yes: build a workflow.
Is it open-ended, verifiable and overseeable?
Yes: build an agent.
Is the work breadth-first and parallel?
Consider subagents, if the value justifies about 15x the tokens.
Rule of thumb If you cannot verify the result, start with a workflow or a human-reviewed assistant, not an autonomous agent.

11  /  How to build

Six steps from idea to working agent

01

Define the task and the finish line

Write what done looks like and how you will check it. If you cannot verify it, you cannot evaluate it.

02

Start with one call

Prompt a single Claude call with retrieval and examples. Keep it as your baseline to beat.

03

Write and test the tools

Few, well-named tools with clear descriptions and compact outputs. Prototype, then evaluate them.

04

Add the loop and stop conditions

Call, run tools, return results, repeat. Add a max step count and a clear done signal.

05

Evaluate on real tasks

Start with about 20 representative queries. Grade outcomes, using an LLM judge with a rubric where output is free-form.

06

Harden, then scale

Permissions, sandbox, human checkpoints, logging and retries. Only then consider subagents or hosted execution.

Frameworks Start by using the LLM API directly. Many patterns take a few lines of code, and extra abstraction layers can hide prompts and responses, which makes debugging harder.

12  /  Code

The loop is short. The tools are the work

Option A   Your own loop on the Messages API
import anthropic
client = anthropic.Anthropic()
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]

for step in range(MAX_STEPS):          # stop condition
    resp = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=4096,
        tools=TOOLS, messages=messages)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant",
                     "content": resp.content})
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":  # model is done
        break
    results = [{"type": "tool_result",
                "tool_use_id": b.id,
                "content": run_tool(b.name, b.input)}
               for b in resp.content
               if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user",
                     "content": results})
Option B   The Agent SDK runs the loop
import anyio
from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions

async def main():
    options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
        allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Bash"],
        permission_mode="acceptEdits",
    )
    async for message in query(
        prompt="Fix the failing tests in ./src",
        options=options,
    ):
        print(message)

anyio.run(main)
Read this Both snippets are illustrative sketches, not drop-in production code. TOOLS, run_tool, task and MAX_STEPS are yours to define. Install with pip install claude-agent-sdk.

13  /  Patterns

Five workflow patterns cover most of the ground

Prompt chaining

Each call feeds the next, with optional gates between.

Fixed subtasks: draft copy, then translate.

Routing

Classify the input, send it to a specialized path.

Support triage; small model for easy, large for hard.

Parallelization

Run independent parts at once, then aggregate. Or vote.

Guardrails beside the answer; multi-pass code review.

Orchestrator-workers

A lead model breaks the task down at runtime and delegates.

Multi-file code changes; research with unknown scope.

Evaluator-optimizer

One call generates, another critiques, loop until good.

Translation nuance; iterative search with clear criteria.

And then, agents

When you cannot predict the steps, drop the fixed structure and let the model direct the loop, using the same building blocks as tools.

Autonomy costs more and needs stronger guardrails.

14  /  Scaling up

Multi-agent systems and context engineering

90.2%better than single-agent Opus 4 on Anthropic's internal research eval (Opus 4 lead, Sonnet 4 subagents)
15xtokens versus chat for multi-agent runs. Single agents use about 4x
90%less research time from parallel subagents and parallel tool calls, on complex queries

Keep the smallest set of high-signal tokens

Recall falls as the window fills, known as context rot.

Just-in-time retrieval

Keep lightweight references such as paths, queries and links, and load data at runtime with tools like grep and glob.

Compaction

Summarize a long history and restart with the summary. Too aggressive and you lose details that matter later.

Structured notes

Have the agent write progress to files outside the window and read them back when needed.

Sub-agents

Delegate focused work to a clean context and take back a condensed result.

Sources [2] [4]AI Agents on Claude    14
15  /  Quality

Tool design and evals decide whether it works

Design tools like an interface for a new hire

Choose the right tools

Fewer, consolidated tools beat a thin wrapper per API endpoint. Do not add tools the agent does not need.

Namespace and name clearly

Group related tools under clear prefixes so boundaries are obvious when many are loaded.

Return meaningful, compact context

Prefer readable names over raw IDs, support concise and detailed response modes, and paginate or truncate large outputs.

Write descriptions as prompts

Spell out inputs, units and edge cases. Small wording changes can move accuracy noticeably.

Evaluate early, on real work

Start small

Around 20 queries that mirror real usage are enough to see big effects early. Do not wait for a huge suite.

Grade outcomes, not exact paths

Agents can reach a good result by different routes. Check the end state and that the process was reasonable.

Use an LLM judge, with a rubric

Score accuracy, citations, completeness and tool use, then spot-check with humans for what automation misses.

Let Claude improve the tools

Paste evaluation transcripts into Claude Code and ask it to refactor tool descriptions against the eval.

16  /  Limits

Where agents still break

01

Cost and latency

About 4x the tokens of chat for agents and 15x for multi-agent. Each loop turn is another model call.

MitigateRoute easy work to smaller models. Set step and token budgets.
02

Errors compound

Agents are stateful and run long. A small failure early can derail everything after it.

MitigateCheckpoints, retries and resumable sessions.
03

Context rot

Recall degrades as the window fills. Long tasks strain the context.

MitigateCompaction, notes in files, or subagents with clean contexts.
04

Coordination overhead

Early multi-agent builds spawned dozens of subagents for simple queries and searched endlessly.

MitigatePut effort-scaling rules in the prompt and cap subagents.
05

Hard to evaluate

Outputs are free-form and the path is non-deterministic.

MitigateAbout 20 real cases, an LLM judge with a rubric, plus human checks.
06

Prompt injection

Content an agent reads can try to steer it into leaking files or running harmful commands.

MitigateSandbox filesystem and network. Grant least privilege.
07

Verification gap

Tests confirm function, but fit with the wider system still needs judgment.

MitigateTests plus human review before consequential actions.
08

Moving target

Tooling and best practice change quickly. Anthropic notes its Dec 2024 landscape has already shifted.

MitigateKeep the loop simple. Re-read the current docs often.
Sources [1] [2] [4] [10]AI Agents on Claude    16
17  /  Safety

Give agents room to work, inside walls

1

Least privilege

Claude Code is read-only by default and asks before edits or commands. Give an agent only the tools and directories it needs.

2

Permissions and approvals

The Agent SDK lets you decide which tools run automatically and which need approval, including a custom permission callback.

3

Sandboxing

OS-level filesystem isolation plus network isolation. You need both: one without the other can be bypassed.

4

Hooks and logs

Run your own code at key points in the agent lifecycle to block, audit or rewrite actions. Keep full event history.

5

Human checkpoints

Pause for approval before consequential actions. Add stop conditions such as a maximum number of iterations or a token budget.

Photo: John K Thorne, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
84%fewer permission prompts in Anthropic's internal use of Claude Code after adding sandboxing, with safer boundaries.

18  /  Checklist

Before you ship an agent

I tried a single well-prompted call with retrieval first
The task has a checkable definition of done
I have a baseline and about 20 real test cases
Tools are few, named clearly, and return compact output
The loop has a max step count and a budget
Permissions, sandbox and approvals match the risk
Failures are logged, retried and resumable
I know my token cost per task and it is worth it
A human reviews anything consequential
I read the current docs, since tooling changes fast

Where to start this week

  1. Pick one task that is verifiable and repeatable.
  2. Build the baseline single call and measure it.
  3. Prototype with the Agent SDK or a 30-line loop.
  4. Add one tool at a time and re-run your evals.
